units.text: The home you make with a partner draws in the younger people around you, and you spend your later years inside the household you built.
You find a partner close to your work or your parents' circle, and the line between your job and your home stays thin for years.
You pass the customs of your first family to the young people you raise or train, and your later years come to resemble your earliest ones.
Your first family stays tied to your working life, and you take a trade or a contact or a loyalty from home into every job you hold.
The young people in your life pull against the home you share with a partner, and you move house or rework your days to keep both.
Work and home compete for the same hours in your life, and you change jobs or addresses when the strain between them gets too loud.
What you built at work in your rising years stops fitting your later life, and you change course in your late forties rather than hold on to it.
Your own household breaks sharply from the one you grew up in, and you keep a partner and your first family at a careful distance.
Nothing from the house you grew up in passes cleanly to the young people after you, and you raise or train them by rules you wrote yourself.
Your choice of work breaks with what your family expected, and you leave home early to make your own way in a trade nobody there chose.
A partner and the young ones you raise or train pull together around one shared aim, and you see your household grow stronger with each passing year.
Your working years feed straight into your home, and you and a partner end up backing the same plan or running something together.
Work, home and the people after you build on each other, and what you start in your rising years keeps growing through every later decade.
The momentum you build at work carries well into your later life, and the people you train along the way become your strongest allies.
Your first family stands behind the home you make, and you build a household with a partner while their help stays close at hand.
You link the house you grew up in to the people after you, and your own home becomes the place where three generations meet.
Something your first family began passes to the young ones after you, and you spend your later years adding to it alongside them.
The household you grew up in gives your working life a running start, and you build on doors your parents or siblings opened for you.
One aim gathers force from your childhood through your working years into your own home, and you carry it from one stage to the next.
Every part of your life adds to one story, from your first home through work and partnership to those who follow you, and you watch it gather weight.
Skills learned at home run through your career into the people you train, and you become the link that carries them forward.
A quiet friction runs between your partner and the people after you, and you spend years smoothing over complaints nobody says out loud.
Late evenings and calls on days off wear quietly at your home life, and you guard one part of every week from your work.
Your work rubs at the people after you in small ways, a missed evening or a forgotten promise, and you make it up to them in person.
An old irritation from your first home follows you into the one you share with a partner, and you settle it one small argument at a time.
Something from your own childhood wears at how you treat the young ones in your care, and you catch yourself repeating it and correct it.
Your family never quite approves of the work you choose, and you answer that quiet doubt with results more than with arguments.
The same argument returns at home between you and the people after you, and you break the loop by changing your own rule first.
You bring the standards of your work home, and a partner meets the same demands you make of colleagues until you draw a line where the job stops.
The pressure you put on yourself at work passes to the people you train, and you ease it once you see them repeat your hardest years.
Old house rules from your childhood come back inside your own home, and you hear them in your voice with a partner and rewrite them one at a time.
You hold the people after you to the standards you were raised on, and the same friction repeats until you decide which of those rules you keep.
Your family's expectations follow you into every job, and you drive yourself harder than any boss asks until you settle on your own measure.
What you struggle with at home reappears in the people after you, and you break the habit in yourself first so they do not inherit it.
You make the same mistake at work and at home, taking on too much and resenting it later, and you catch it sooner each time it returns.
A habit that holds you back at work returns in your later life, and you see it coming the second time and turn it down.
The quarrel you grew up around repeats in your own home with a partner, and you end it by changing your own part in it.
Your childhood plays out again around the young ones in your care, and you recognise the old scene early enough to give it a different ending.
The role you played in your family returns at work, the peacemaker or the one who carries everything, and you change it once you see it twice.
